analysis.one_liner: Bans new offshore oil and gas leasing within 100 miles of Florida's coast.
analysis.headline: Introduced June 25, 1998 by Florida's two senators and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the same day, the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred the Interior Department from offering any new oil and gas leases in the Eastern Gulf of Mexico, the Straits of Florida, and the South Atlantic within 100 miles of Florida's coast. Drilling on leases that already existed could continue only after completed, peer-reviewed environmental studies and a report certifying the science was adequate. It also created a joint federal-state task force dominated by Florida's governor's appointees and gave Florida a say in approving any offshore development plans.
analysis.who_benefits: Florida's coastal communities: residents, beach-town tourism businesses, and commercial and recreational fishing interests that depend on an unpolluted coastline. The state government also gains, because the bill requires Florida's concurrence before offshore development plans can be approved.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Florida coastal communities and tourism economies

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the Interior Secretary from conducting any preleasing activity or holding any lease sale in the Eastern Gulf of Mexico, Straits of Florida, and South Atlantic planning areas within 100 miles of Florida's coast.

Allows exploration, production, or drilling on existing leases only after all required environmental, ecological, and socioeconomic studies are completed, peer-reviewed by qualified scientists supervised by a joint federal-state task force, and certified to Congress and Florida's governor as adequate with a minimal level of uncertainty.

Establishes a Joint Federal-State Outer Continental Shelf Task Force — including six representatives of Florida appointed by its governor — to guide environmental studies, resolve conflicts between Florida and federal agencies, and peer-review required research.

Requires state concurrence before any Development and Production Plan or Development Operations Coordination Document can be approved, subjects exploration plans to full National Environmental Policy Act review, and gives affected states the final environmental impact statement months before they must respond.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies, which would lose access to new federal leases off Florida and face new study requirements and state sign-offs before working existing leases. The federal treasury would forgo any lease-sale revenue those areas might have generated.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not cancel leases issued before enactment; drilling on them can proceed once the study and certification hurdles are met, so the protection for already-leased areas is conditional, not absolute.

It permanently removes those federal waters from leasing, forgoing domestic oil and gas production and the lease-sale revenue that leasing would have produced — a real cost in a country that relies on offshore production for part of its energy supply.

By requiring state concurrence for federal development approvals and letting states treat their consistency responses as provisional until studies are complete, the bill gives a single state effective veto power over federal energy decisions and could allow review requirements to delay projects indefinitely — a fair objection from anyone who thinks offshore energy is a national, not purely state, concern.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Florida's coast, the benefits are concrete: a leasing ban protects beaches, fisheries, and a tourism economy that an oil spill could damage for years, and the extra scientific review on existing leases addresses real gaps the National Research Council had already flagged. The costs are forgone energy production and federal revenue, plus a significant shift of power from the federal government to one state. Weighed plainly, the bill traded potential offshore drilling revenue for protection of a coastline that supports a large resident and visitor economy — a trade most Floridians supported, which is why its death in committee mattered to them.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Sen. Bob Graham (D-FL) introduced the Florida Coast Protection Act on June 25, 1998, for himself and Sen. Connie Mack (R-FL).
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote, before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies kept the existing federal leasing process intact, with no new barriers to activity off Florida's coast from this bill; the Energy and Natural Resources Committee's inaction preserved the status quo.

for.name: Sen. Bob Graham
for.role: U.S. Senator from Florida, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: Sen. Connie Mack
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; Graham introduced it on behalf of both Florida senators.

against.name: Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources
against.what_they_did: Received the referred bill and took no action on it — no hearing, markup, or report — for the remaining six months of the Congress.

against.name: Sen. Frank Murkowski
against.role: Chair, Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair in the 105th Congress, never scheduled the bill for committee consideration, letting it die without action.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — a Florida Democrat and a Florida Republican — reflecting a state, not a partisan, coalition; the obstacle it faced was committee inaction, not a floor vote.

industries.note: The bill blocks new federal lease sales in three planning areas within 100 miles of Florida and layers peer-reviewed study requirements and state concurrence onto existing leases. The industry's interest in opening these waters runs against coastal communities whose economies would bear the risk of spills.
A leasing ban protects the beaches, reefs, and clean water that draw visitors and support coastal economies. Their gain comes directly from keeping drilling rigs away from shore.
Keeping new drilling out of the Eastern Gulf and South Atlantic protects fisheries and fishing grounds from the disruption and spill risk that offshore development brings.
